Examples

Co-op Arena — Godot engine multiplayer

6 min readOdin × GodotPage source ↓
On this page ↓
One codebase, three modesAuthority and damage rulesScene replication requirements from tests/repl_spikeHeadless test coverageDeploying internet co-op (room-code lobby)Deployment and playtesting limitsFiles

For the Kit multiplayer toolkit, start with examples/cavecrawl or examples/slopball. Co-op Arena demonstrates direct use of Godot's MultiplayerSynchronizer and @(gd_rpc) APIs in ~1,100 lines of networking code. Kit supplies corresponding integration for its examples.

This pure-Odin / Polygon2D survivors game runs in three modes: single-player, native ENet co-op, and browser WebRTC co-op. Each player simulates their own pawn and projectiles locally, so movement and firing do not wait for a host round-trip. Peers trust the firing player's damage reports.

examples/survivors remains the single-player gameplay reference; its co-op layer is retained as the host-authoritative engine-native variant and as regression coverage for engine replication interop; see its README.

Code
nix develop --command bash -c 'bash examples/coop_arena/run.sh'              # single-player  -> ARENA_SINGLE_OK
nix develop --command bash -c 'bash examples/coop_arena/coop_native_run.sh'  # co-op ENet      -> ARENA_NATIVE_OK
nix develop --command bash -c 'bash examples/coop_arena/coop_web_run.sh'     # co-op WebRTC    -> ARENA_WEB_OK

To play windowed: open the project in Godot and press Single Player, Host, or Join on the start screen (WASD to move; weapons auto-fire at the nearest enemy).

One codebase, three modes#

The same arena_player.odin, arena_bullet.odin, arena_enemy.odin and the ArenaGame orchestrator (arena.odin) run in all three modes:

  • Single-player uses the host simulation. It opens no transport, and broadcasts have no remote recipients.
  • Transport is chosen at compile time by platform: native builds use ENet (gd.host / gd.join); the web build uses WebRTC (gd.webrtc_host / gd.webrtc_join / gd.webrtc_poll). The same @(gd_rpc) methods and gd.rpc calls work over either, once connected.
  • A scripted session, selected by native COOP_ROLE or the web ?role= query, drives the headless test scenario. With no role, the game shows its start screen.

Authority and damage rules#

Each player's pawn has its multiplayer authority assigned to the owning peer, including its child MultiplayerSynchronizer. The owner simulates movement and auto-fire locally each frame; other peers display its synchronized transform. Local input therefore does not wait for a host round-trip. The check in arena_player.odin is if !node_is_multiplayer_authority(owner) { return }.

When a peer fires, it creates its bullet locally and broadcasts fired(origin, dir). Other peers create visual ghost bullets with the same path. Only the firing peer's bullet resolves hits. It applies and broadcasts damage through the damage RPC with call_local, and peers trust those reports. The host does not validate hits; this cooperative policy provides no anti-cheat protection against a dishonest firing peer.

The host creates enemies through MultiplayerSpawner and moves them toward the nearest pawn. Each client's spawner instantiates the matching scene, and MultiplayerSynchronizer sends the host's position and spawn-once id. Enemies have no player input awaiting a local response, so their movement can follow the host.

Damage remains peer-authoritative. Each peer stores enemy hp locally and subtracts the broadcast damage from the firing player. The host owns the enemy's multiplayer authority and frees dead enemies; the spawner replicates despawn. hp is deliberately excluded from the synchronizer configuration because damage RPCs update it.

A possible scaling change for hundreds of enemies is to broadcast spawn seeds and simulate the horde locally on each peer, sending only deaths afterward. That would require deterministic enemy simulation. This example instead streams host positions; it does not benchmark the alternative's capacity.

Scene replication requirements from tests/repl_spike#

  • SceneReplicationConfig is configured in the .tscn (a SubResource referenced by the MultiplayerSynchronizer), never built in _ready. See arena_player.tscn / arena_enemy.tscn.
  • The MultiplayerSpawner is built on every peer in _ready (the client's spawner is what instantiates the host's spawns).
  • The host's queue_free of an enemy is not paired with an explicit despawn RPC — the spawner replicates the despawn; an explicit RPC would double-free (ERR_UNAUTHORIZED).

Headless test coverage#

mode sentinel proves
single ARENA_SINGLE_OK unified codebase solo: move, auto-fire kills, XP/level, contact death
native (ENet) ARENA_NATIVE_OK Connection, both owner-authoritative pawns visible on both peers, owner movement replication, enemy spawn/position sync, local bullet on the firing tick (BULLET_LOCAL) followed by the remote bullet (BULLET_REMOTE), matching peer-authoritative kill/credit, despawn replication, and firing player's XP
web (WebRTC) ARENA_WEB_OK The same owner-authoritative cases in two browsers over WebRTC; ARENA_WEB_BUNDLED records a skip when Chrome/puppeteer is unavailable

The "OWNER-LOCAL IMMEDIACY" check uses a firing client. It logs BULLET_LOCAL on the frame its auto-fire timer fires; the host logs BULLET_REMOTE after the broadcast arrives. This checks that the local bullet appears before a round-trip to the host could complete.

Deploying internet co-op (room-code lobby)#

The web build pairs two players through a room-code lobby. To use it across networks, provide a signaling server reachable by both players:

  1. Run a signaling relay reachable by both players at wss://HOST/rtc and implementing the JSON protocol below. A Node reference is provided at tests/webrtc/signal_server.mjs; the original deployment notes also report an Elixir implementation of the same protocol in production.
  2. The host opens the page, sets the signaling URL, presses Host, and shares the displayed room code, such as WATR.
  3. The other player opens the page, enters the code, and presses Join. Both enter the arena when the WebRTC data channel connects.

The signaling URL is configurable: the lobby's URL field, or on web the ?url= query (?url=wss://HOST/rtc); the join code is the room field or ?room=CODE. Single-player is unchanged (no transport, no lobby).

Signaling wire protocol (raw WebSocket, JSON text frames; server path /rtc)#

Code
client -> server                                  server -> client
  {"type":"create"}                                 {"type":"created","room":"<CODE>","id":1}
  {"type":"join","room":"<CODE>"}                   {"type":"joined","room":"<CODE>","id":<n>}
  {"type":"signal","to":<peerId>,"data":<opaque>}   {"type":"peer","id":<peerId>}
  {"type":"leave"}                                  {"type":"signal","from":<peerId>,"data":<opaque>}
                                                    {"type":"peer_left","id":<peerId>}
                                                    {"type":"error","reason":"no_room"|"full"|"bad_msg"}

The server relays data (the SDP offer/answer + trickled ICE) verbatim — it never parses it. The host (id 1) creates the offer; the joiner answers. Implemented client-side in godot/Ergonomics_WebRtc.odin (mirrored in bindgen/upstream/godot/) via Godot's WebSocketPeer

  • JSON; the same @(gd_rpc) layer then runs over the resulting WebRTCMultiplayerPeer.

STUN / TURN#

Ergonomics_WebRtc.odin configures the WebRTCPeerConnection with a public STUN server (stun:stun.l.google.com:19302) so peers behind ordinary NATs gather server-reflexive candidates. For symmetric-NAT pairs that STUN can't punch, add a TURN relay (with credentials) to the _ICE_CONFIG_JSON iceServers array — there's a documented slot. Localhost (host candidates) needs neither, which is why the headless tests don't require STUN.

Deployment and playtesting limits#

Headless tests cover local bullet response, replication, and peer-authoritative kills in all three modes. The browser tests exercise host create, code sharing, join, and WebRTC RPC across two local browsers (WEBRTC_OK / ARENA_WEB_OK). They do not establish internet NAT traversal or play quality under real latency.

Those checks require two machines on different networks, a public wss://HOST/rtc relay, and a TURN server for symmetric NAT. Localhost tests do not exercise those paths. Playtesting must also assess response and presentation on the deployed connection.

Files#

  • scripts/arena.odin — the ArenaGame orchestrator (transport, start screen, pawn spawn, host enemy spawner, the headless scripted session, and the fired / damage / spawn_pawn RPCs).
  • scripts/arena_player.odin — the owner-authoritative pawn (local movement + auto-fire).
  • scripts/arena_bullet.odin — the owner-simulated / deterministic-local projectile.
  • scripts/arena_enemy.odin — the shared-horde enemy (host position, peer-auth hp).
  • scripts/util.odin, scripts/boot.odin — shared helpers + the verbatim cross-DLL init.
  • arena.tscn, arena_player.tscn, arena_enemy.tscn, arena_bullet.tscn — scenes (the replication config lives in the pawn/enemy .tscn).
  • run.sh, coop_native_run.sh, coop_web_run.sh, coop_drive.mjs — the three test harnesses.
